edition.window: Orders and decisions passed or reported between 10:00 AM IST on 25 November 2026 and 10:00 AM IST on 26 November 2026

items.caseName: Shree Varun Infratech v. Jigar Pradipchandra Shah & Ors.
items.coram: Justice Yogesh Khanna (Judicial Member) and Barun Mitra (Technical Member)
items.headline: NCLT cannot order fresh valuation after CoC approves resolution plan merely because approval is delayed
items.text: The NCLAT held that a corporate debtor's assets cannot be revalued simply because approval of a CoC-approved resolution plan has been delayed, absent any statutory or procedural defect. Review under Section 31 IBC is confined to checking compliance with Section 30(2) and does not allow second-guessing the CoC's commercial wisdom. The NCLT's order was set aside and the approval application remitted for decision, preferably within 60 days.

items.caseName: Vijay Kumar Agarwal v. Balajidham Build Estate Pvt. Ltd.
items.coram: Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan (Judicial Member) and Naresh Salecha (Technical Member)
items.headline: Courts must prefer adjudication on merits unless grave prejudice is caused: NCLAT revives recall application
items.text: The NCLAT set aside an NCLT order of 6 May 2026 that refused to restore a recall application dismissed for counsel's non-appearance, calling the approach excessively rigid. It noted the NCLT had denied time to file a reply without reasons despite a credible explanation for the absence. The application was revived and remanded for a fresh hearing of both sides.

items.caseName: Harri Wind Farms v. Suzlon Energy Ltd.
items.coram: Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma (Judicial Member) and Arun Baroka (Technical Member)
items.headline: NCLAT gives Suzlon Energy three weeks to reply to operational creditor's appeal against CIRP rejection
items.text: The NCLAT granted Suzlon Energy three weeks to respond to Harri Wind Farms' appeal against the NCLT Ahmedabad's dismissal of its Section 9 insolvency petition. The NCLT had found that the creditor had not fully performed its obligations under the MoU and development agreement and that its legal notices were time-barred. Both sides must file written submissions before the next hearing in the second week of January.

items.coram: Prabhat Kumar (Technical Member) and Sushil Mahadeorao Kochey (Judicial Member)
items.headline: Co-borrower's liability cannot be treated as a personal guarantee under IBC
items.text: NCLT Mumbai held that being a co-borrower on a separate loan does not by itself make a person a personal guarantor, so each obligation must be assessed under its own contract. It rejected Axis Finance's objection that the petition was meant to obstruct SARFAESI recovery, holding such steps do not bar a Section 94 filing. The personal insolvency petition was admitted under Section 100 IBC.

items.caseName: Metro Infratech v. Jaishnavi Eminence Pvt. Ltd.
items.coram: Manni Sankariah Shanmuga Sundaram (Judicial Member) and Reena Sinha Puri (Technical Member)
items.headline: Contractor cannot claim royalty separately if it is included in quoted rates
items.text: NCLT Delhi held that royalty could not be claimed separately because the work order deemed it included in the contractor's quoted rates. Retention money of Rs 2.61 crore was also excluded, since it fell due only after the defect liability period ended, well after the claimed default date. The balance of about Rs 4.13 lakh fell below the Rs 1 crore threshold, so the Section 9 petition was dismissed.

items.caseName: Arun Kumar Mishra (Personal Guarantor) v. Hindustan Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
items.coram: Manni Sankariah Shanmuga Sundaram (Judicial Member) and Reena Sinha Puri (Technical Member)
items.headline: Company debts alone cannot justify insolvency proceedings against an alleged personal guarantor
items.text: NCLT Delhi held that unpaid debts of corporate borrowers do not by themselves justify personal insolvency proceedings against an alleged guarantor. Lenders must first show the contractual basis of the guarantee and the individual's exposure under it. With no guarantee deed or personal demand on record, the tribunal rejected the RP's recommendation and dismissed the Section 94 application.

items.caseName: Globe Enterprises (India) Limited & Morabia Creations Limited
items.coram: Chitra Hankare (Judicial Member) and Dr. V. G. Venkata Chalapathy (Technical Member)
items.headline: NCLT Ahmedabad admits first-motion application for Globe Enterprises-Morabia Creations demerger
items.text: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted a joint first-motion application and directed Globe Enterprises to convene shareholder and creditor meetings within 45 days on the proposed demerger of its trading business. Morabia Creations was excused from a shareholders' meeting as all ten shareholders consented in writing, and it has no creditors. Notices were ordered to the Regional Director, RoC, SEBI, BSE and NSE.

items.caseName: Cella Warehousing Private Limited v. Income-tax Officer
items.coram: Vimal Kumar (Judicial Member) and Ramit Kochar (Accountant Member)
items.headline: ITAT Delhi treats foreign parent's Rs 41.65 crore FCCDs in Indian subsidiary as equity for transfer pricing
items.text: The ITAT upheld treating Rs 41.65 crore of FCCDs issued to the Singapore parent as equity and sustained a nil arm's length price for interest, leading to a Rs 4.58 crore adjustment. It relied on the parent's minimal equity, thin capitalisation and interest accruing regardless of profits. The appeal was dismissed, but rectification of a double addition of interest already disallowed under Section 94B was directed, subject to verification.

items.headline: ITAT deletes Rs 2.97 crore disallowance on Hero MotoCorp Chairman's foreign travel
items.text: The Delhi bench deleted a Rs 2.97 crore disallowance relating to the Chairman's 2014 trip to Colombia and the US, which the AO had partly treated as personal because family members accompanied him. The tribunal found no additional charter cost arose from the family's presence. It held that the Revenue had not shown the expenditure was personal in nature.

items.headline: Section 151 approval is a condition precedent to reopening, not an administrative formality: ITAT quashes reassessment
items.text: The Mumbai ITAT held that sanction under Section 151 is a mandatory precondition for reopening an assessment. It quashed the Section 148 reassessment for AY 2015-16 because approval was given by an officer other than the authority specified in Section 151(2). The Revenue's appeal against deletion of additions under Sections 69 and 69A thus failed.

items.caseName: Vinod Prabhudayal Agrawal (legal heir of late Rama Vinod Agrawal)
items.headline: Section 96 of RFCTLARR Act overrides Section 56(2)(viii): interest on enhanced compensation for acquired land not taxable
items.text: The Pune ITAT held that Section 96 of the RFCTLARR Act, 2013 overrides Section 56(2)(viii) of the Income Tax Act. Interest received on enhanced compensation for agricultural land compulsorily acquired by NHAI was therefore exempt and could not be taxed as income from other sources. The addition for AY 2018-19 was deleted.

items.headline: Addition cannot rest on unsigned third-party Excel sheet: ITAT deletes Rs 32 lakh addition despite high-risk flag
items.text: The Rajkot ITAT deleted a Rs 32 lakh Section 69 addition for AY 2019-20 that rested solely on an unsigned Excel sheet seized in a search of a real estate group. The AO had treated alleged on-money for a flat as undisclosed income after reopening the case. The tribunal held the addition could not stand without corroboration and an opportunity of cross-examination.

items.headline: AO cannot go beyond show cause notice to deny Section 80GGC political donation deduction
items.text: The Delhi ITAT deleted an addition denying a Rs 7.66 lakh Section 80GGC deduction for AY 2024-25 for cheque donations to two registered unrecognised political parties. It held the AO could not rely on search findings that were not put to the assessee in the show cause notice. The disallowance was set aside.

items.caseName: Wockhardt Limited v. Commissioner of Central GST & Central Excise, Vadodara-II
items.coram: Somesh Arora (Judicial Member) and Satendra Vikram Singh (Technical Member)
items.headline: EOU status and alleged safety lapses cannot bar duty remission for goods destroyed in fire
items.text: CESTAT Ahmedabad allowed Wockhardt's appeal, finding the April 2010 fire at its Ankleshwar unit was accidental. It held that alleged safety lapses and 100% EOU status could not bar duty remission, and allowed remission on destroyed machinery and raw materials, including indigenous goods under Rule 21 of the Central Excise Rules. Demands, interest and penalties were set aside, though Wockhardt must explain a Rs 15.32 lakh reconciliation gap.

items.caseName: Sansin Enterprises & Ors. v. Commissioner of Customs, Chennai-II
items.caseNo: Customs Appeal Nos. 40704 to 40706 of 2019 and 40404 to 40406 of 2019
items.coram: P. Dinesha (Judicial Member) and Vasa Seshagiri Rao (Technical Member)
items.headline: CESTAT Chennai sets aside customs duty demand on 60 bills of entry based on discrepancies in 10
items.text: CESTAT Chennai set aside a duty demand because discrepancies found in 10 bills of entry were extended to all 60 without linking them to the disputed imports. Proforma invoice values had been treated as final without addressing the importer's explanation of later price cuts, and no evidence supported the alleged extra freight. Penalties under Sections 112(a) and 114AA were set aside and the Revenue's appeals dismissed.

items.caseName: Mrs. Jagyanseni Dash, Managing Director, M/s Jagynaseni Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. v. Mrs. Jharashree Das & Odisha Real Estate Regulatory Authority
items.caseNo: OREAT Appeal No. 160/2024 (arising out of C.C. No. 54 of 2023)
items.coram: S.K. Rajguru (Judicial Member) and Dr. B.K. Das (Technical and Administrative Member)
items.headline: Promoter cannot cancel allotment after accepting over 10% without registered sale agreement
items.text: The Odisha REAT held that a developer could not unilaterally cancel a flat allotment and refund the buyer after collecting over 10% of the price without executing a registered agreement for sale. This breached Sections 13(1) and 14(1) of the RERA Act, and the refund did not extinguish the buyer's right to the agreement. The appeal was dismissed and the price recalculated proportionately for the revised carpet area.
